newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco industry says Florida sold cigarettes. [CORRECTED 09:35 GMT, 25/01]
newsitem.headline: Tobacco industry says Florida sold cigarettes. [CORRECTED 09:35 GMT, 25/01]

text.p: Lawyers for the tobacco industry argued Friday that cigarette-makers should be allowed to present evidence in a landmark trial that the state sold cigarettes to prisoners and must bear responsibility for smoking-related illnesses of its citizens.

The motion to allow the evidence was filed in the state's court case to try and recover $450 million in Medicaid payments for smoking-related illnesses. A jury trial in the case is scheduled to begin this summer.
The tobacco industry claimed Florida must bear the cost of smoking-related illnesses because it had permitted the use and sale of tobacco in the state.

"The State of Florida for several years in the mid- to late 1970s manufactured, sold and gave away cigarettes to inmates within its prisons and to patients within its hospitals, as well as counties and municipalities," said attorney Stephen Krigbaum, who represents the industry.

The documents presented by lawyers for Brown & Williamson, R.J. Reynolds and Philip Morris Cos. Inc. showed that the Florida department of Offender Rehabilitation operated a cigarette manufacturing factory at a state prison and distributed cigarettes free of charge to state inmates.
Lawyers for the tobacco industry also claimed that during the first quarter of fiscal year 1977, the state reported a net profit of more than $81,000 on total cigarette income of $174,373.

Lawyers for the industry want the court to grant permission for cigarette-makers to use the so-called "affirmative defense" that claims the state was partly to blame for smoking and benefitted from it. The industry contends that the state of Florida sells cigarettes to youths in state institutions and has profited from the sales.
Robert Montgomery, an attorney for the state, said Florida law prohibits cigarette-makers from using actions by individuals or Florida to avoid being sued for damages.

"The tobacco industry owns the (Florida) legislature. That's why it has been able to successfully oppose every piece of legislation that would keep teenagers from smoking," Montgomery said in an interview before the hearing.
Tobacco industry lawyers said they would also ask the court to bar the state from seeking triple damages under the racketeering law, should the state eventually win its $450 million lawsuit.
It was not known whether Circuit Court Judge Harold Cohen would rule immediately on the motions, or issue a decision at a later date.
R.J. Reynolds is a division of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp., and Brown & Williamson is owned by B.A.T Industries PLC.
